title: Counter-Attack and Other Poems
description: Sassoon's war book at its most bitter: 'Counter-Attack', 'Suicide in the Trenches' and 'Everyone Sang'.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Counter-Attack', 'Suicide in the Trenches', 'The Rear-Guard', 'Does It Matter?', 'Aftermath' and the great lyric 'Everyone Sang' — the poems of the soldier's hatred, the trench and the dead.
narrative_structure: A collection of war poems and satires.
principal_characters: The rear-guard; the soldier; the general
historical_context: The last year of the First World War and Sassoon's return to the front after Craiglockhart.
literary_significance: Counter-Attack is the central collection of Sassoon's war poetry: 'Suicide in the Trenches' and 'The Rear-Guard' are among the most powerful anti-war poems in English, and 'Everyone Sang' is one of the great poems of the armistice.

title: The Collected Poems of Wilfred Owen
description: The greatest body of war poetry in English: 'Dulce et Decorum Est', 'Strange Meeting' and the pararhyme.
plot_or_argument: The collection gathers the some two dozen finished poems and the fragments: 'Anthem for Doomed Youth', 'Dulce et Decorum Est', 'Strange Meeting', 'Futility', 'Mental Cases', 'Exposure', 'Spring Offensive', 'The Send-Off' and 'Insensibility'.
narrative_structure: Some two dozen finished poems and fragments, with the famous prose preface.
historical_context: The First World War, Craiglockhart and Sassoon's encouragement, the London Blitz of the Somme and Serre in 1917, and Owen's death on the Sambre canal a week before the armistice.
literary_significance: Owen's Collected Poems is the greatest body of war poetry in English: his two dozen finished poems changed the language of war poetry, his pararhyme gave modern verse a new technique, and 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and 'Strange Meeting' are permanent national texts. His preface — 'the Poetry is in the pity' — is the period's definitive statement of the poet's duty.
bibliographical_notes: Published as Poems in 1920 (ed. Sassoon) and The Poems of Wilfred Owen in 1931 (ed. Blunden); the standard edition is C. Day-Lewis's Collected Poems (1963), superseded by Stallworthy's Complete Poems and Fragments (1983).

title: Poems (Rosenberg, 1922)
description: The war poetry of the ranks: 'Break of Day in the Trenches', 'Dead Man's Dump' and the visionary fragments.
plot_or_argument: The collection gathers Rosenberg's poems from Night and Day (1912) through the war poems: 'Break of Day in the Trenches', 'Dead Man's Dump', 'Returning, We Hear the Larks', 'Louse Hunting', 'August 1914' and the visionary 'Daughters of War'.
narrative_structure: The collected poems, including the verse play Moses and the war fragments.
historical_context: The Jewish East End of London, the Slade School, and the First World War, in which Rosenberg served in the ranks and was killed at Arras in April 1918.
literary_significance: Rosenberg's Poems is the greatest body of war poetry written from the ranks: 'Break of Day in the Trenches' and 'Dead Man's Dump' are among the finest war poems in the language, and his visionary fragments show an ambition cut off at twenty-seven.

title: Good-bye to All That
description: The great English war memoir: Charterhouse, the trenches, the wound that was reported as death, and the flight from England.
plot_or_argument: Graves recounts his childhood and public school, his enlistment in 1914, the trenches of the Royal Welch Fusiliers, the Somme and the wound of 1916 that was reported as his death, the shell shock of his recovery, and his post-war Oxford and marriage — and ends with his departure for Majorca and his farewell to England.
narrative_structure: Chronological autobiography in chapters, from childhood to the departure for Majorca.
principal_characters: Robert Graves; his family; Siegfried Sassoon; the Royal Welch Fusiliers
historical_context: The First World War and its aftermath, Charterhouse and the English public-school system, and the literary London of the 1920s.
literary_significance: Good-bye to All That is one of the two great English memoirs of the First World War and the book that changed the writing of autobiography: its irony, its detail and its refusal of consolation made it the model for the war books boom of 1929.

title: Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man
description: Sassoon's finest prose: a country childhood in the hunting field, told as a novel, before the war arrives.
plot_or_argument: George Sherston grows up in the Kent and Sussex countryside before 1914: the hunting field, the point-to-point, the groom Dixon, the cricket and the county society — and the memoir ends with the outbreak of the war, which will take him to the trenches in the two following volumes.
narrative_structure: A first-person memoir-novel in two parts: the country childhood and the coming of the war.
principal_characters: George Sherston; Dixon; Aunt Evelyn; Denis Milden; Stephen Colwood
historical_context: The English county families and the hunting field before 1914, and the war that ended them.
literary_significance: Memoirs of a Fox-Hunting Man is the finest English prose memoir of the war and one of the great English books about a lost world: its country childhood is the equal of any in English, and its structure — the idyll before the war — made it the model for the war books of 1929.

title: Undertones of War
description: The most lyrical prose memoir of the First World War: the Western Front seen by a country poet.
plot_or_argument: Blunden records his service in the Royal Sussex Regiment from 1916 to 1918 — the Somme, Ypres, Passchendaele — in prose that moves like a country walk, noting the weather, the birds, the ruined villages and the dead, without protest and with an unbroken attention to the visible world.
narrative_structure: Prose memoir in chapters, followed by a section of thirty-two war poems.
principal_characters: Blunden; his battalion; the ruined villages; the landscapes of the Somme and Ypres
literary_form: War memoir (with a section of poems)
historical_context: The First World War and the English countryside from which Blunden came, and the war books boom of 1928–29 in which it appeared.
literary_significance: Undertones of War is the most beautiful prose memoir of the First World War: its pastoral attention and its refusal of rhetoric make it the perfect counterweight to Good-bye to All That, and its poems are among the finest of the war.

title: The Everlasting Mercy
description: The poem that caused a scandal by using the word 'bloody': a poacher's conversion in the Herefordshire countryside.
plot_or_argument: Saul Kane, a brutal poacher and drunkard, is converted by a Quaker preacher's daughter and by a vision in the fields, and the poem follows his fight with the collier Bill Gasser and his slow conversion in the Herefordshire countryside.
narrative_structure: A long narrative poem in rhymed couplets.
principal_characters: Saul Kane; Bill Gasser; the Quaker preacher; Jane
historical_context: The Herefordshire countryside of Masefield's childhood, the agricultural labourer's world, and the Edwardian debate about realism in poetry.
literary_significance: The Everlasting Mercy revived the English narrative poem and caused a national scandal: its use of the word 'bloody' in a serious poem made it a literary event, and its story of conversion gave the period its finest narrative poem of country life.

title: Salt-Water Ballads
description: Masefield's first book and the source of 'Sea-Fever': the sailor's ballad and the English sea lyric.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Sea-Fever', 'A Wanderer's Song', 'Trade Winds', 'The Golden City of St Mary' and the sailor's ballads of the forecastle, the brothel and the voyage.
narrative_structure: Twenty-three ballads and lyrics of the sea.
historical_context: Masefield's own years at sea, the English merchant marine, and the revival of the ballad in the 1890s.
literary_significance: Salt-Water Ballads gave the period its most popular sea poetry: 'Sea-Fever' — 'I must go down to the seas again' — is one of the best-known English poems of the century, and the collection revived the sailor's ballad as a modern form.

title: The Collected Poems of Rupert Brooke
description: The whole of Brooke's verse gathered in the year of his death: the Georgian lyrics and the 1914 sonnets.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Brooke's poems from 1905 to 1914 — 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester', 'The Great Lover', 'Heaven', 'Dust', the South Seas poems and the five war sonnets.
narrative_structure: Collected poems with an introduction by Henry James and a memoir.
historical_context: The Cambridge and Grantchester of the pre-war years, the Pacific travels of 1913–14, and the war that made him famous.
literary_significance: The Collected Poems of Rupert Brooke is the monument of the Georgian generation: published in the year of his death, it sold in tens of thousands and fixed the image of the golden English poet who died for his country.

title: Songs of Childhood
description: De la Mare's first book: the songs and riddles of the nursery, published under a pseudonym.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Song of the Mad Prince', 'The Horseman', 'The Sleepy Miller', 'The Wondrous Ballad' and the nursery songs that established his voice — the first appearance of the child's world that Peacock Pie would perfect.
narrative_structure: Some fifty nursery songs and riddles.
historical_context: The Edwardian nursery and the golden age of the illustrated children's book.
literary_significance: Songs of Childhood is the first book of the greatest English writer of children's verse: published under the pseudonym Walter Ramal, it began the body of nursery poetry that Peacock Pie would perfect, and it is one of the permanent children's books in English.

title: Eminent Victorians
description: The book that invented modern biography: Manning, Florence Nightingale, Arnold and General Gordon, reduced to human size.
plot_or_argument: Strachey's four short lives — Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold of Rugby and General Gordon — use irony, psychology and the revealing scene to dismantle the Victorian ideal of the great man, and the book ends with Gordon's death at Khartoum.
narrative_structure: Four separate lives, each with a preface and a short bibliography.
principal_characters: Cardinal Manning; Florence Nightingale; Thomas Arnold; General Gordon
historical_context: The First World War, which had destroyed the Victorian world the book dismantles, and the Bloomsbury reaction against Victorian earnestness.
literary_significance: Eminent Victorians invented modern biography: its irony, its psychological penetration and its use of the revealing detail changed how lives are written, and every twentieth-century biographer who debunks or humanises a subject works in its debt.

title: Queen Victoria
description: The finest short life in English: Victoria, Albert, Melbourne and Disraeli, and the private life behind the public monument.
plot_or_argument: Strachey follows Victoria from a lonely childhood through the accession, the domination of Lord Melbourne, the marriage to Albert, the widowhood of forty years, the highland servant John Brown, the Indian secretary Disraeli and the Diamond Jubilee, ending with her death in 1901.
narrative_structure: Ten chapters from 1819 to 1901, with an epilogue.
principal_characters: Queen Victoria; Prince Albert; Lord Melbourne; Disraeli; John Brown; the Duchess of Kent
historical_context: The Victorian age and its aftermath, and the Bloomsbury reaction against the public pieties of the previous century.
literary_significance: Queen Victoria is the most admired short life in English and won the James Tait Black Prize: it made the Victorian age intelligible as a private life and established the modern literary biography as an art.

title: Vision and Design
description: The book that brought modern art into English criticism: the formalist essay and the case for Post-Impressionism.
plot_or_argument: The essays — 'An Essay in Aesthetics', 'Art and Socialism', 'The Art of the Bushmen', 'Negro Sculpture', 'Giotto', 'The French Post-Impressionists' — argue for the primacy of form over subject and defend the art that Fry had exhibited in 1910 and 1912.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five essays written over twenty years, arranged thematically.
historical_context: The Post-Impressionist exhibitions of 1910 and 1912, the Bloomsbury art world, and the English resistance to modern art.
literary_significance: Vision and Design made modern art intelligible to English readers: its formalism gave English criticism a method, its defence of Post-Impressionism changed the taste of a generation, and it is the founding book of modern English art criticism.

title: Pointed Roofs
description: The first English stream-of-consciousness novel: a young woman goes to Germany to teach and the world is rendered from inside her mind.
plot_or_argument: Miriam Henderson, a shabby-genteel English girl of seventeen, goes to a German finishing school to teach English. The novel records her impressions — the school, the town, the other teachers, the music, the humiliation and the freedom — entirely through her consciousness, in the continuous present of perception.
narrative_structure: Continuous present-tense interior monologue in thirteen chapters.
principal_characters: Miriam Henderson; the Fräulein; the school; the German town
historical_context: The English and German boarding schools of the 1890s, and the restricted life of the educated but poor woman of the period.
literary_significance: Pointed Roofs is the first English stream-of-consciousness novel, preceding Ulysses by seven years: it gave English fiction the sustained interior monologue, and it is the founding text of the novel of female consciousness that Woolf and Mansfield would develop.

title: The Good Soldier: A Tale of Passion
description: The most perfect English novel of the period: a study of deception told by a narrator who is himself deceived.
plot_or_argument: John Dowell, a wealthy American, recounts the nine years he and his wife Florence spent at Nauheim with their friends Edward and Leonora Ashburnham — the 'good soldier' of the title — and slowly reveals the adulteries, the lies and the cruelties beneath the surface, including his own blindness and Florence's suicide.
narrative_structure: Four parts in a broken chronology narrated by Dowell, with deliberate repetitions and withholdings.
principal_characters: John Dowell; Florence Dowell; Edward Ashburnham; Leonora Ashburnham; Nancy Rufford; Maisie Maidan
historical_context: The Edwardian upper class and its conventions, the European spa of the pre-war years, and the code of honour that conceals everything.
literary_significance: The Good Soldier is the most perfect English novel of the period and the great novel of unreliable narration: its broken chronology, its narrator's self-deception and its famous opening — 'this is the saddest story I have ever heard' — made it the model for the modern novel of deception.

title: Some Do Not…
description: The first volume of the great English war tetralogy: Christopher Tietjens, the last Tory, and the end of Edwardian England.
plot_or_argument: Christopher Tietjens, a brilliant statistician in the Imperial Department of Statistics, is married to the unfaithful Sylvia and in love with Valentine Wannop, a suffragette. The novel moves between the golf course at Rye, the London of the war office and the trenches of the Western Front in 1917, and ends with Christopher's return to England and the collapse of his marriage.
narrative_structure: Two parts: the pre-war England and the Western Front of 1917.
principal_characters: Christopher Tietjens; Sylvia Tietjens; Valentine Wannop; Vincent Macmaster; General Campion; Mrs Duchemin
historical_context: Edwardian England before 1914 and the Western Front of 1917, the suffrage movement and the official class.
literary_significance: Some Do Not… opens the greatest English war novel: its portrait of Christopher Tietjens as the last English gentleman, its technical brilliance and its picture of a society destroying itself made Parade's End the finest English novel of the war and the transition to modern England.

title: Parade's End
description: The greatest English novel of the First World War: Tietjens, the trenches and the end of the old England, in four volumes.
plot_or_argument: The tetralogy — Some Do Not… (1924), No More Parades (1925), A Man Could Stand Up (1926) and The Last Post (1928) — follows Christopher Tietjens through the collapse of his marriage, his service on the Western Front, his love for Valentine Wannop, and his post-war life in the Sussex countryside, and ends with the birth of his child and the death of his brother Mark.
narrative_structure: Four volumes: two pre-war and war, two war and post-war.
principal_characters: Christopher Tietjens; Sylvia Tietjens; Valentine Wannop; Mark Tietjens; Marie Léonie; General Campion
historical_context: The First World War and the Edwardian world it destroyed, from the golf links of Rye to the mud of the Somme and the peace of a Sussex farm.
literary_significance: Parade's End is the greatest English novel of the First World War and the finest study of the transition from Edwardian to modern England: its technical innovation, its portrait of Tietjens as the last gentleman and its movement from the war to the peace made it a permanent work.

title: The Garden Party and Other Stories
description: Mansfield's finest collection: the garden party, the doll's house, the fly and the last stories of loss.
plot_or_argument: The title story sets a wealthy garden party against the death of a carter in the lane below; the collection also contains 'The Doll's House', 'The Fly', 'Her First Ball', 'At the Bay' and 'The Voyage' — stories of childhood, family, marriage and grief.
narrative_structure: Fifteen stories, several set in the same New Zealand world.
principal_characters: Laura Sheridan; the workmen; Kezia Burnell; the boss; the fly
historical_context: The New Zealand of Mansfield's childhood and the England of the war and after, written while she was dying of tuberculosis.
literary_significance: The Garden Party is the summit of Mansfield's art and one of the finest short-story collections in English: 'At the Bay' and 'The Garden Party' changed the form, and the collection's exact surface with its hidden grief is the model for the modern story.

title: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle
description: The greatest long poem in Scots: a drunk man's night on a hillside with a thistle, and the whole condition of Scotland.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, drunk, lies on a hillside beside a thistle and holds a night-long argument with it: about Scotland, Calvinism, the Scots language, love, drink, the industrial city, communism, the universe and his own soul, in a sequence of lyric passages and dramatic monologues that moves between Scots and English.
narrative_structure: A night-long sequence of lyric and dramatic passages in Scots and English.
historical_context: The Scotland of the 1920s: the industrial depression, the loss of the Scots language, the Calvinist inheritance, and the nationalist revival of the Scottish Renaissance.
literary_significance: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is the greatest long poem in Scots and the founding work of the Scottish Renaissance: it restored Scots as a modern literary language, made the condition of Scotland the subject of a great poem, and is one of the permanent long poems of the century.

title: Sunset Song
description: The finest Scottish novel of the century: Chris Guthrie, the Mearns farming country, and the destruction of a world by war and the machine.
plot_or_argument: Chris Guthrie grows up on a croft in the Mearns, is torn between her mother's Scots and her father's English, watches her family break up and her father die, marries the farmer Ewan Tavendale, and loses him to the First World War. The novel ends with the village dead of the war, the farms sold, and Chris leaving for the city.
narrative_structure: Four parts (Prelude, The Song, The Woman, Epilude) with choric openings.
principal_characters: Chris Guthrie; Jean Guthrie; John Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Chae Strachan; Long Rob
historical_context: The farming country of the Mearns between 1911 and 1919, the First World War, and the agricultural depression that emptied the land.
literary_significance: Sunset Song is the finest Scottish novel of the century and one of the great novels of rural dispossession in English: its Scots-inflected prose, its choric parish voice and its elegy for a destroyed world made it a permanent classic.
